Gardener
GARD-nur
n. (one who tends a garden; what Mary supposed the risen Christ to be)
From Old French jardinier, from jardin, a garden — ultimately from a Germanic root meaning an enclosure. In John it renders Greek kepouros, literally a garden-keeper, from kepos, garden, and ouros, a watcher.

Biblical Definition

Mary Magdalene stands weeping outside an empty tomb, and the risen Lord asks her why she weeps and whom she seeks. She, supposing him to be the gardener, saith unto him, Sir, if thou have borne him hence, tell me where thou hast laid him, and I will take him away. It is one of the great near-misses of Scripture, and the mistake is more fitting than she knew. There was a garden in the place where he was crucified, and in the garden a new sepulchre; the man she took for its keeper was the one who had planted the first garden and put a man in it to dress it and to keep it. The whole story of Scripture runs from a garden where a man was driven out to a garden where a woman was told, go to my brethren. Jesus takes garden language for himself constantly: I am the true vine, and my Father is the husbandman; the dresser of the vineyard pleading one more year for a barren fig tree; the sower, the seed, the harvest, the wheat and the tares. Mary was not wrong about his trade. She was only wrong about which garden he was keeping, and how recently he had come out of the ground.

Webster 1828 Definition

Webster (1828): one whose occupation is to make, tend and dress a garden; one skilled in gardening.

expand to see more

GARDENER, n. One whose occupation is to make, tend and dress a garden.

GARDEN, n. A piece of ground appropriated to the cultivation of herbs, fruits, flowers or plants of any kind.

DRESSER, n. One who dresses; one who prunes and tends vines or trees.

SEPULCHRE, n. A grave; a tomb; the place in which the dead body of a human being is interred.

HUSBANDMAN, n. A farmer; a cultivator or tiller of the ground.

Key Scripture

John 20:15 — "Jesus saith unto her, Woman, why weepest thou? whom seekest thou? She, supposing him to be the gardener, saith unto him, Sir, if thou have borne him hence, tell me where thou hast laid him, and I will take him away."

John 15:1 — "I am the true vine, and my Father is the husbandman."

Luke 13:7 — "Then said he unto the dresser of his vineyard, Behold, these three years I come seeking fruit on this fig tree, and find none: cut it down; why cumbereth it the ground?"

Genesis 3:23 — "Therefore the LORD God sent him forth from the garden of Eden, to till the ground from whence he was taken."

Modern Corruption

The resurrection is treated as a symbol of renewal that the seasons already teach; John reports a woman who could not find a body, argued with a stranger about where it had been moved, and then heard her own name.

expand to see more

Spring is the standard modern reading of Easter: life returns, as it always does, and the resurrection is the church's way of saying so. John's account resists this at every point. Mary is not meditating on renewal; she is looking for a corpse and offering to carry it herself. The tomb is a real tomb with grave clothes lying in it and a napkin folded separately. The conversation is mundane to the point of awkwardness — she takes him for staff and asks about logistics. Nothing here is a seasonal metaphor. Paul stakes everything on the difference: if Christ be not raised, your faith is vain, ye are yet in your sins, and we are of all men most miserable.

The fitting thing about Mary's error, though, should not be lost to the argument. He was in a garden, and he does keep gardens. He planted one and walked in it in the cool of the day; he calls his Father the husbandman and himself the vine; he stood in another garden the night before and sweat as it were great drops of blood. The gospel begins with a man driven out of a garden and turns, at a grave in a garden, when a gardener says one word — Mary — and she knows him.

Greek & Hebrew Roots

Greek kepouros (G2780), a garden-keeper; kepos (G2779), a garden; georgos (G1092), a husbandman or vinedresser; Hebrew gan (H1588), a garden.

expand to see more

Greek kepouros (G2780) — a keeper of a garden; used once in Scripture, and mistakenly.

Greek kepos (G2779) — a garden; John notes there was one in the place where he was crucified.

Greek georgos (G1092) — a tiller of the soil, a vinedresser; my Father is the husbandman.

Hebrew gan (H1588) — a garden, an enclosure; Eden, and the garden of Gethsemane's counterpart.

Hebrew abad (H5647) — to work, to serve, to till; the man was put in the garden to do it.

Usage

"“supposing him to be the gardener” — a mistake more fitting than she knew."

"“my Father is the husbandman” — the trade claimed in plain words."

"“to till the ground from whence he was taken” — the first man sent out of the first garden."
